header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, LAHORE
Khurram Shahzad Vs. The State, etc.
Order with signature of judge, and that of parties or
17.11.2026. Mr. Javed Iqbal Bhatti, Advocate for petitioner.
Mr. Hamaad Iftikhar Syed, DDPP for State.
Mr. Nasir Mehmood Mangat, Advocate for respondent
body: Khurram Shahzad (petitioner), through the instant criminal revision, has called in question the orders dated 24.06.2026 and 17.07.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Mandi Bahauddin, whereby the earlier order dated 10.12.2025 regarding the unblocking of the passport of proforma respondent No.4 (Faheem-ur- Rehman) was recalled, the surety bond in the sum of Rs.20,00,000/- furnished by the petitioner on behalf of the said accused was ordered to be forfeited to the State, proceedings under Section 514, Cr.P.C. were initiated for recovery of the forfeited amount and, subsequently, the immovable property of the petitioner/surety was ordered to be attached.

2. Briefly, the facts giving rise to the instant petition are that proforma respondent No.4, namely Faheem-ur- Rehman alias Bholu, is facing trial in a private complaint relating to FIR No.90/2010, dated 24.02.2010, registered under Sections 302, 34 and 109, PPC, at Police Station Saddar, Mandi Bahauddin. He was declared a proclaimed offender and his passport bearing No.AQ8151001 was ordered to be blocked. Subsequently, the petitioner, Khurram Shahzad, who is the brother of proforma respondent No.4, approached the learned Sessions Judge, Mandi Bahauddin, through an application under Sections 22-A and 22-B, Cr.P.C., seeking the unblocking of the passport of the said accused to enable him to return to Pakistan and face the criminal proceedings. The said application was disposed of vide order dated 10.12.2025, subject to the furnishing of a surety bond in the sum of Rs.20,00,000/- by the petitioner and a direction that the accused would appear before the Court within two months from the date of unblocking of his passport, failing which the complainant would be at liberty to seek forfeiture of the surety bond. The accused, however, failed to appear before the learned Trial Court within the stipulated period. Consequently, respondent No.2 moved an application seeking forfeiture of the surety bond and recall of the earlier order. The learned Trial Court, vide order dated 24.06.2026, accepted the application, recalled the earlier concession granted for unblocking of the passport, ordered forfeiture of the surety bond and initiated proceedings under Section 514, Cr.P.C. for recovery of the forfeited amount. Thereafter, the petitioner was afforded an opportunity to explain his default; however, his reply was found unsatisfactory and, vide the subsequent order dated 17.07.2026, the learned Trial Court directed attachment of his immovable property. Hence, the instant revision petition.

3. Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the accused could not return to Pakistan as he was allegedly deported by the Italian authorities to Greece and remained in the custody of the Greek authorities. It is argued that the absence of the accused/respondent No.4 was beyond the control of the petitioner and, therefore, the forfeiture of the surety bond was unjustified. Learned counsel further submits that the impugned orders are contradictory to the earlier order dated 10.12.2025 and that the attachment of the petitioner's immovable property is not sustainable under Section 514, Cr.P.C. It is also contended that the petitioner has been subjected to double punishment and that the impugned orders have been passed without lawful justification 4. Conversely, the learned Law Officer as well as learned counsel for respondent No.2 support the impugned orders and submit that the petitioner failed to ensure the appearance of the accused despite having furnished a substantial surety bond.

6. In the instant case, the controversy essentially revolves around the question whether the petitioner, having furnished a surety bond to secure the appearance of proforma respondent No.4, can escape the consequences of forfeiture merely on the ground that the absence of the said respondent was beyond his control. A perusal of the order dated 10.12.2025 reveals that the concession of unblocking the passport of the accused was granted on an application voluntarily filed by the petitioner, who gave a specific undertaking, duly secured before the Court through a surety bond of Rs.20,00,000/-, and assured the Court that his brother/accused intended to appear before the learned Trial Court within two months. The said condition was neither vague nor ambiguous. The petitioner, knowing its consequences, voluntarily furnished the surety bond and was bound to ensure compliance with its terms. Admittedly, the accused failed to appear before the learned Trial Court within the stipulated period, as undertaken by the petitioner, and thereby failed to avail the concession extended to him for the specific purpose of facilitating his return to Pakistan to face the criminal proceedings. The explanation offered by the petitioner, that his brother was deported from Italy to Greece and remained in the custody of the Greek authorities, does not by itself absolve him of the responsibility undertaken through the surety bond. A mere assertion in the reply to the show-cause notice, without satisfactory substantiation, was not sufficient to discharge the obligation undertaken by him. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has consistently held that the provisions of Section 514, Cr.P.C. are to be adhered to strictly and that, where the person whose appearance has been secured fails to appear, the surety is liable to forfeiture of the bond unless sufficient cause is shown [ ]. The contention that the learned Trial Court had no authority to recall the earlier order dated 10.12.2025 is equally misconceived, as the said order was conditional in nature and the benefit extended to the petitioner's brother thereunder was expressly dependent upon the appearance of the said accused within the prescribed period. When that condition was not fulfilled, the learned Trial Court was competent to examine the consequences of such default and rightly proceeded in accordance with law. The subsequent order dated 24.06.2026, therefore, cannot be termed an arbitrary exercise of jurisdiction merely because it recalled the earlier conditional concession. A person who takes advantage of an order which both grants a benefit and imposes a burden cannot accept the former and reject the latter [ ]. Likewise, the plea of double punishment is devoid of force, as the recall of the conditional concession and the proceedings for forfeiture of the surety bond are consequences arising from the failure to fulfil the obligation undertaken by the petitioner as surety, and do not constitute punishment for the same offence twice [ ].

[ ] Ghulam Dastagir and 3 others v. The State (PLD 2011 SC 116); Saeed Akhtar v. The State (2009 SCMR 834); Zeeshan Kazmi v. The State (PLD 1997 SC 267). [ ]Asrar Ahmed and others v. Chairman Pakistan Aeronautical Complex Board, Kamra and others (2023 SCMR 1427)

[ ] Article 13(a) of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973 and Section 403, Cr.P.C. protect a person against being prosecuted or punished more than once for the same offence. So far as the objection regarding the attachment of the petitioner's immovable property is concerned, it may be observed that the impugned order dated 17.07.2026 was passed in continuation of the proceedings initiated for recovery of the forfeited amount, and the petitioner has not been able to demonstrate, at this stage, any independent adjudication of his proprietary rights or any material showing that the revenue authorities have acted beyond the authority conferred upon them by law. It is also noteworthy that the petitioner himself approached the learned Sessions Court seeking the unblocking of his brother's passport and voluntarily furnished a substantial surety bond to secure his appearance. Having availed himself of the benefit of the conditional order, he cannot now dissociate himself altogether from the undertaking furnished by him [ ]. No patent illegality, material irregularity or jurisdictional defect warranting interference by this Court in its revisional jurisdiction has been pointed out by learned counsel for the petitioner.

It is pertinent to mention here that the petitioner, Khurram Shahzad, through Writ Petition No.59303 of 2026, titled “Khurram Shahzad vs. The State, etc.”, called in question the order dated 16.09.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, Mandi Bahauddin, with the following assertions: - “Briefly stated, the record reflects that Faheem-ur-Rehman alias Bholo was facing proceedings in case arising out of FIR No.90/2010 under sections 302, 109 and 34 PPC, Police Station Saddar, Mandi Bahauddin. He was declared a proclaimed offender vide order dated 14.02.2011, whereafter his passport was blocked. Subsequently, the petitioner, being his brother, approached the learned Court seeking unblocking of the passport so that the proclaimed offender could return to Pakistan and surrender before the Court. The learned Court, vide order dated 10.12.2025, extended a conditional indulgence by directing temporary unblocking of bond under Section 514, Cr.P.C. enforces the surety's own undertaking; it is not the punishment of an offence.

The petitioner furnished the requisite surety bond and, on the strength of the said undertaking, the passport of the proclaimed offender was temporarily unblocked. The record further reveals that despite availing the concession extended by the learned Court, the proclaimed offender neither returned to Pakistan nor surrendered before the Court within the stipulated period. Consequently, vide order dated 24.06.2026, the concession earlier granted was recalled and the surety bond was ordered to be forfeited to the State and proceedings under section 514 Cr.P.C. were thereafter initiated against the petitioner/surety. The petitioner was duly served with a show-cause notice and was afforded an opportunity to explain his position. His written reply was considered by the learned Court, but was found not satisfactory, therefore, vide order dated 09.07.2026, the learned Court accordingly directed the petitioner to deposit the forfeited amount of Rs.2,000,000/- and proceeded further in accordance with law. Upon his failure to comply of abovesaid order with regard to deposit of said surety amount, proceedings for recovery/attachment of his property were initiated and in pursuant to the subsequent directions of the learned Court, the competent Revenue Authorities submitted compliance reports confirming attachment of the immovable property measuring 15 Kanals 13 Marlas, belonging to the petitioner/surety. Likewise, the Passport Authority confirmed that the passport of the proclaimed offender had been duly blocked and its status reflected as “Not Active”. The learned Court, vide impugned order dated 16.09.2026, considered the compliance reports and found that the directions issued earlier had been duly implemented.”
The said writ petition was dismissed in limine by this Court vide order dated 05.10.2026.

8. For what has been discussed above, finding no merit in the instant criminal revision petition, the same is dismissed. Consequently, the impugned orders dated 24.06.2026 and 17.07.2026 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Mandi Bahauddin, are maintained.
